findings.issue: The separate rhetorical question introducing the final argument is omitted.
findings.suggested_revision: Insert a corresponding question before “Even if,” for example: “And what of this? Even if it was difficult for you to know what God is…” Submit the revision for fresh review.

findings.source_quote: ἢ γὰρ οὐχ ὑπὸ σιδήρου ἐτορνεύθησαν, — καὶ ὁ τορνεύσας σίδηρος ὑπὸ πυρὸς ἐμαλάχθη —
findings.english_quote: Were they not shaped by iron—and was not the iron that shaped them softened by fire
findings.issue: Both forms of τορνεύω are reduced to generic shaping. The verb's turning or lathe-working image is not represented or explained.
findings.suggested_revision: Compare the draft explicitly with wording retaining the workmanship, such as “Were they not shaped on a lathe by iron—and was not the iron that shaped them on the lathe softened by fire…?” If broader “shaped” is retained, document its contextual justification and preserve the turning/lathe-working sense in a source-quoted lexical note. Any replacement requires fresh review.

findings.source_quote: καὶ τρηδόνας ἐποίησεν, ἵνα σοι παράσχῃ πηγὰς
findings.english_quote: He made openings so that it might provide springs for you
findings.issue: The subject of παράσχῃ is unexpressed. “It” selects a nonpersonal antecedent, apparently the earth, whereas God, the subject of ἐποίησεν, is also a viable subject. The supplied note explains the openings but neither identifies the intended antecedent nor discloses this alternative. The earth reading is defensible; the problem is incomplete disclosure, not source corruption.
findings.suggested_revision: Identify the intended antecedent and add a source-quoted note explaining the choice. If the earth is intended, note its connection with the preceding ἡ γῆ and preserve the alternative “so that he might provide springs for you,” with God as subject.

findings.source_quote: τὸ δὲ ὕδωρ ὑπὸ πνεύματος κινήσεως τὴν γένεσιν λαμβάνει
findings.english_quote: water receives its coming into being through the movement of spirit
findings.issue: The main text takes πνεύματος as dependent on κινήσεως and treats γένεσις as the water's coming into being. Another defensible attachment takes ὑπὸ πνεύματος together and κινήσεως with γένεσιν: water receives the beginning of its motion from spirit or wind. That alternative accords closely with the water-motion statement in 11.22. The existing note discusses wind versus spirit but does not disclose the materially different existence-versus-motion readings or explain the chosen attachment. The supplied reading admits defensible English and does not require source emendation.
findings.suggested_revision: Add a source-quoted note preserving both attachments and explaining the contextual reason for the selected one. Alternatively, submit “water receives the beginning of its motion from spirit” as a proposed replacement for fresh review, retaining the wind alternative and documenting the grammatical choice.

findings.source_quote: ἵνα ἐπὶ λόγῳ εἰς θεὸν καταντῆσαι δυνηθῇς, ὅπως ἐπιγνῶς σου τὸ γένος καὶ πρωτογόνῳ ἀναγεννηθῇς ὕδατι καὶ κληρονόμος καταστῇς τῶν πρὸς ἀφθαρσίαν γεννησάντων σε γονέων.
findings.english_quote: so that through reason you may be able to reach God, recognize your lineage, be born again through first-born water, and become an heir of the parents who begot you for incorruptibility.
findings.issue: The draft flattens the two successive purpose constructions into one coordinated list under “may be able to.” It does not represent the second purpose link introduced by ὅπως, which follows reaching God and introduces recognizing one's lineage, rebirth, and inheritance.
findings.suggested_revision: Restore the second purpose construction, for example: “so that through reason you may be able to reach God, in order that you may recognize your lineage, be born again through first-born water, and become an heir of the parents who begot you for incorruptibility.” This proposed wording requires fresh review.
